cards.title: Fine-grained comparability of permanent and SETH
cards.formal: Are exact binary-matrix permanent computation and the family of fixed-width satisfiability problems comparable by deterministic fine-grained oracle reductions at the \(2^n\) scale? Ask whether at least one of the following two fixed directions exists. In the SAT-to-permanent direction, for every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), there is a rational \(0<\delta<1\), independent of the clause width, such that for every fixed \(k\ge3\) a reduction decides \(k\)-SAT on \(n\) variables, using an exact binary-permanent oracle, with ordinary bit time \(T\) and queried matrix dimensions \(N_j\) satisfying \[T+\sum_j2^{(1-\varepsilon)N_j}\le C\,2^{(1-\delta)n}(L+1)^a.\] Here \(L\) is the formula encoding length, and \(C,a\) and the reduction may depend on \(\varepsilon,k\). In the permanent-to-SAT direction, for every rational \(0<\varepsilon<1\), there exist rational \(0<\delta<1\), a fixed \(k\ge3\), and a reduction computing the permanent of every \(N\times N\) binary matrix using a \(k\)-SAT decision oracle, with queried variable counts \(n_j\) and \[T+\sum_j2^{(1-\varepsilon)n_j}\le C\,2^{(1-\delta)N}(N+1)^a.\] In this direction \(\delta,k,C,a\) and the reduction may depend on \(\varepsilon\), but not on \(N\) or the matrix. A single direction must satisfy its condition for every \(\varepsilon\).
cards.why: The permanent is a canonical exact counting problem with a natural exponential algorithm, whereas SETH organizes the difficulty of satisfiability decision across clause widths. A quantitatively efficient connection would reveal whether their exponential barriers have a common source. Ordinary counting completeness does not determine how a constant improvement in one exponential base transfers to the other problem.
cards.status_note: The either-direction comparison is posed in the checked 2013 source. Later primary work supplies precise reduction conventions and a distinct arithmetic-circuit connection, but no verified resolution of this binary-matrix deterministic comparison was found in bounded checks through 2026-09-16. The fully specified reducibility target is a documented interpretation of the source, not an assertion that all informal hardness comparisons are equivalent.

sentences: The permanent of a binary matrix counts its perfect matchings exactly.
The source asks whether its exponential-time difficulty can be related to SETH in either direction.
This card makes that comparison precise using deterministic oracle reductions that preserve a constant saving in the exponential rate.
A reduction from SAT must preserve a saving uniform across clause widths, while the reverse direction may choose a fixed width for each saving.
The preferred binary-matrix case and exact counting oracle are distinguished from general matrix variants, ordinary completeness and counting SAT.

cards.definitions:
For \(A\in\{0,1\}^{N\times N}\), \(N\ge1\), define \(\operatorname{per}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_N}\prod_{i=1}^N A_{i,\pi(i)}\), where \(S_N\) is the set of permutations of \([N]=\{1,\ldots,N\}\). The exact integer, between zero and \(N!\), is returned in binary. Encode the input as \(1^N0\) followed by its \(N^2\) entries in row-major order. The parameter is the matrix dimension \(N\), not the number of entries or nonzero entries. For fixed \(k\), \(k\)-SAT asks whether a conjunction of clauses, each a disjunction of at most \(k\) signed Boolean variables from a declared set of \(n\ge1\) variables, has a satisfying assignment. Empty clauses are allowed. Remove tautological clauses and duplicate literals and clauses; a clause never contains both signs of a variable. Use this concrete canonical encoding: prefix \(1^n0\), followed by one bit for each possible normalized clause of size at most \(k\), indicating whether it occurs. Order these clauses first by size, then lexicographically by their increasing lists of variable indices and signs, with negative sign before positive sign. The formula length is \(L=n+1+\sum_{j=0}^{\min(k,n)}2^j\binom nj\), polynomial in \(n\) for each fixed \(k\). Unused declared variables are permitted. A queried SAT instance uses the same fixed \(k\) and encoding. This representation fixes all encoding choices; ordinary sparse representations differ by only polynomial factors for fixed \(k\).

A reduction is a deterministic multitape oracle Turing machine with a finite program for its stated fixed parameters, no advice and no random bits. It must be correct on every valid input when its oracle returns the correct value. It may make finitely many adaptive calls, meaning later calls may depend on previous answers. The permanent oracle returns the exact binary integer, while the SAT oracle returns only the YES/NO decision, not a witness or a satisfying-assignment count. The ordinary time \(T\) counts all machine transitions, including writing queries, processing answer bits, preprocessing, arithmetic and final output; only the internal oracle computation is excluded. The displayed sum charges every oracle call separately at its hypothesized improved exponential cost. The constants satisfy \(C\ge1\), \(a\in\mathbb N\), and the bound must hold on every valid input. No effective dependence of a reduction program on the external constant \(\varepsilon\) or on \(k\) is required; each chosen machine itself is uniform over input lengths. The forward quantifiers are \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta\,\forall k\,\exists R,C,a\). The reverse quantifiers are \(\forall\varepsilon\,\exists\delta,k,R,C,a\). In neither direction may an exponent improvement shrink with the input length.

For context, deterministic SETH asserts that there is no constant \(\eta>0\) for which every fixed \(k\ge3\) has a deterministic \(k\)-SAT algorithm in time \(2^{(1-\eta)n}n^{O(1)}\); the polynomial exponent and algorithm may depend on \(k\). The binary-permanent hypothesis here means that no constant \(\eta>0\) permits exact permanent computation in time \(2^{(1-\eta)N}N^{O(1)}\). The reduction target is explicit quantitative reducibility, rather than the bare propositional disjunction of two implications between these hypotheses. The polynomial factors are harmless under the universal quantification over exponent savings: an algorithm with a fixed larger saving can supply the oracle budget for a smaller saving.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked family of reductions satisfying one of the two directions, including exact correctness and the stated ordinary-time-plus-oracle-cost bounds for all parameters and inputs, or a complete Lean proof that neither direction exists. A positive answer must identify the direction and its quantifier dependence. Polynomial-time counting completeness without the exponential budget, a reduction using a counting-SAT oracle in the reverse direction, or a forward saving \(\delta\) depending on \(k\) is insufficient. A conditional obstruction to a restricted reduction model establishes only that obstruction.

context_blocks.text: Cygan’s seminar question asks for a relation in either direction and explicitly prefers binary matrices. This card keeps both directions as one comparability question and selects that preferred matrix domain. The explicit oracle budgets are a documented fine-grained interpretation of the source’s informal hardness comparison; general weighted matrices remain a different version.

A SAT-to-permanent reduction of the stated strength would make a fixed exponential improvement for permanent contradict SETH. A permanent-to-SAT reduction would make a failure of SETH yield a fixed exponential improvement for permanent. The two directions have different clause-width quantifiers.

The question concerns constructing reductions with a resource guarantee. Merely asking whether one of two unqualified logical implications holds would lose that content: the disjunction of the implications between any two propositions is classically tautological.

Belova and coauthors define fine-grained reductions by charging the sum of the improved running-time budgets over all oracle calls. Their SETH-hardness definition requires a saving independent of the SAT clause width. These conventions motivate the precise forward direction here.

The same SODA 2024 work relates strong co-nondeterministic lower bounds for Binary Permanent to lower bounds for explicit arithmetic polynomial families. That is a distinct conditional connection, not a proof of either deterministic SAT/permanent reduction demanded here.

checked_sources: Read the primary seminar report Section 6.12 on printed page 66, including its either-direction wording and binary-matrix preference.
Read Belova et al. arXiv:2307.11444v1 Sections 2.1 and 2.6; recovered the sum-of-query-cost definition and the clause-width-independent saving needed for SETH hardness.
Read Theorem 5.1 and the Binary Permanent portion of Section 5; its co-nondeterministic lower-bound consequence does not establish a deterministic reduction to or from SAT.

Checked each transfer logically: the forward common delta across k would turn fast permanent into a common SAT saving; the reverse may select a fixed k after epsilon because failure of SETH gives a common saving for every fixed k.

Canonical fixed-width formula lengths are polynomial in their variable count, and the universally quantified saving absorbs polynomial oracle factors by taking a smaller saving. The reverse oracle is decision SAT, never #SAT.
Bounded subsequent-result searches through 2026-09-16 did not verify either complete reduction direction. Broad matrix variants and conditional circuit barriers were kept separate.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Top 100 is a priority subset of those same 500, with secondary editorial attention. Both use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The existing Top 1000 view is not an active benchmark goal. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The legacy Top 1000 view has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Inactive records are archived outside the catalogue, exports and editorial work. Their content, stable IDs and reasons are retained; imports cannot reactivate them. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The primary target is 500 problems; Top 100 is its priority subset with secondary editorial attention. Top 100, Top 500 and the legacy Top 1000 view use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Inactive cards, including resolved records, are archived outside the ranking without changing their historical importance score.
